KEY MESSAGE 1...Windswept rain with minor coastal flooding/beach 
erosion  continues Monday. Localized urban and street flooding 
possible. 

The center of circulation according to nighttime satellite imagery 
and surface observations early this morning is sitting on the New 
Jersey coast. Regional radar shows bands of precipitation continuing 
to be pulled north and west into southern New England this morning. 
Over the next 12-18 hours the low will weaken and lift north, 
passing over SNE this evening and into the Gulf of Maine on Tuesday. 
Thus, not expecting a wholesale change in conditions today. What 
we've got out there now...low clouds, off-and-on showers, breezy 
winds...will be the story the rest of the day. Now that damaging 
wind concerns are done, the primary hazard is potential flooding 
from additional rainfall. SNE has received anywhere from 1"(western 
MA) to 5-7" (RI and southeast MA) over the last 2-3 days. Even 
though the dynamics aren't as impressive as they were, the 
atmosphere remains very moist with PWATs approaching 1.5"; we could 
squeeze out an additional 1-1.5 inches in some locations before rain 
tapers off Monday night. Thus, the Flood Watch remains in effect. 
Urban and poor drainage flooding will be possible under the heaviest 
downpours, and few small rivers and streams will continue to rise 
into minor flood stage including the Taunton River at Bridgewater. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Minor coastal flooding continues through Monday 
evening.

The secondary concern behind the additional rainfall is for pockets 
of minor coastal flooding owing to the continued northeast winds and 
high astronomical tides. Fortunately several tide gauges including 
Boston Harbor and Nantucket have managed to remain just below flood 
stage overnight. However, Monday afternoon's astronomical high tide 
is higher than Sunday's so given the still expected ~1.5' of storm 
surge we will continue to monitor for minor coastal flooding during 
Monday's high tide (morning along the south coast, early afternoon 
for the east coast). 

KEY MESSAGE 3...Conditions improve Tuesday, followed by mainly dry 
and warmer weather through Friday. Forecast confidence decreases 
next weekend.

The weekend's long-duration nor'easter exits east-northeast as the 
mid-level flow becomes less amplified and blocking diminishes. 
Through the remainder of the week, the mid-level flow becomes fairly 
zonal with a few weaker impulses passing through during the mid to 
late week. These may bring a low probability of a light shower or 
two, but otherwise mainly dry weather is expected. Expect marked 
improvement Tuesday as the decaying nor'easter exits the region and 
winds shift to the northwest. This northwest flow will advect lower 
PWATs into southern New England, bringing any lingering early 
morning showers to an end. While PWATs remain somewhat elevated into 
the afternoon, there is little forcing to support additional 
precipitation. Thus, clouds may hang tough through much of the 
afternoon before some breaks develop later in the day. Northwest 
flow will also keep temperatures a few degrees below climatological 
normals, though it will be noticeably warmer than this past weekend. 
Highs Tuesday reach the upper 60s to around 70 degrees.

A mid-level ridge builds across the southeastern CONUS this week, 
while surface high pressure settles south of the region Wednesday 
through Friday, leading to a stretch of quieter and warmer weather. 
Guidance hints at a weak northern-stream shortwave Wednesday night 
into early Thursday, followed by a secondary shortwave Thursday 
night into Friday. PWATs Wednesday night into Thursday remain below 
1.2 inches and do not align particularly well with the best forcing. 
Outside of a brief light shower, would anticipate more clouds than 
anything. PWATs increase to around 1.5 inches Thursday night with 
the passage of the secondary weak shortwave, when a few light 
showers could brush the region. No significant impacts are 
anticipated with either disturbance. Temperatures trend warmer 
through the middle and latter half of the week, though the latest 
guidance has trended somewhat cooler compared to previous runs. 
Highs generally return to the lower and middle 70s, with Thursday 
potentially the warmest day as temperatures reach the middle to 
upper 70s. No notable cold is expected overnight, with lows 
generally falling into the 50s.

Forecast confidence decreases next weekend due to considerable 
disagreement among the guidance. Interestingly, some solutions 
depict a setup somewhat similar to earlier this week, with another 
strong area of high pressure over eastern Canada and low pressure 
developing off the Carolinas. Other guidance instead settles the 
high over New England while low pressure develops across the Ohio
